title: Conference on Open Science for Innovation | UNESCO
content:
"UNESCO will convene the Open Science for Innovation Conference at its Headquarters in Paris on 12 November 2026, to examine how open science partnerships can support the implementation of the UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science...

The Conference explores four cross-cutting questions:


	Designing openness into partnerships  How can open science, open science partnerships and intellectual property be combined with intention and sequenced across the research to application pathway, so that they reinforce rather than undermine one another?
	Evidence from UNESCO priority areas What do selected partnerships in fields such as water and biodiversity research show about governance, funding and accountability, and about measurable progress in their respective fields?
	Openness and research security How can concerns for the security and integrity of research and data can be addressed without narrowing who is able to take part in science
	Policy levers in government hands How can governments use funding, procurement and data policy to encourage open science and open science partnerships?"

title: Towards the Shape of Responsible Research Metrics: A Hybrid Citation-Mapping Approach to Scientific and Policy Uptake
content: Research metrics have become deeply embedded in science, despite sustained criticism of their limitations and unintended effects, especially in research assessment. Key reform documents such as the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment, the Leiden Manifesto, and The Metric Tide established core principles for the responsible use of metrics and shaped broader debates on responsible research assessment. This research-inprogress paper maps the scientific and policy uptake of these foundational documents through a hybrid citationmapping approach, combining bibliographic data from Web of Science, Scopus, and OpenAlex with policy citation data from Overton. At this stage, the analysis focuses on the scientific corpus, examining its temporal development, geographical distribution, and citation-overlap patterns. Preliminary findings highlight the prominent position of the Leiden Manifesto, limited overlap among the three foundational documents, and broad international diffusion centred in Europe and North America, with Asia playing an increasingly important role.

title: Awareness and Integration of FAIR principles in Research Data Management by LIS researchers of Pakistan | Qualitative and Quantitative Methods in Libraries
content: Abstract: Purpose The presence and implementation of FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable) principles is a source of providing transparency and accessibility to the research, avoiding repetitive tasks of researchers. While developed countries are much aware of it and implementing policies for the accessibility of data under a protected environment, it is essential to inquire into the present condition of practicing FAIR principles in developing states to overcome research data sharing problems. Design/methodology The researchers were asked about their research data sharing practices, their awareness, and their implementation of FAIR principles in research activities. A total of 300 respondents were approached for the purpose. SPSS was used for the descriptive statistics, such as mean frequency, and cross-tabulation was performed to analyze the responses. Findings The findings revealed that the researchers have an awareness of the components of FAIR principles, but are not willing to apply them. title: AI, open science, and the extraction imperative: A situated approach to the normativities of open research data | Cambridge Forum on AI: Culture and Society | Cambridge Core
content: Abstract: Open Science has long been framed as a normative project grounded in values of transparency, accessibility and collaboration. Yet in the age of generative AI, many research data practitioners, who once championed openness, are increasingly questioning how these commitments can be upheld when openness also enables undesired large-scale data extraction, decontextualization and enclosure. This paper examines how the normativities of openness are being re-negotiated, and how researchers navigate the ethical and political tensions that arise when their work is repurposed for proprietary AI systems. Drawing on in-depth qualitative interviews, I explore how situated ethical reasoning informs decisions about data sharing. Participants described new risks and dilemmas, from uncontrolled scraping and heightened re-identification threats to the reframing of FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles as pipelines for AI-readiness. Their accounts reveal openness as a relational and contested practice, embedded in specific institutional, infrastructural and community contexts, and continuously re-balanced between care, accountability and collaboration. title: Förderprogramm: „Open-Access-Publikationsförderung“ | DFG
content:
From Google's English:  "The "Open Access Publication Funding" program provides a fixed grant for the publication of research articles and scholarly books in Open Access. The approved grants can be used to cover the total Open Access publication fees incurred by an institution. With this funding, the DFG fulfills its share of the financial responsibility within the framework of (virtual) information and publication budgets.

Grants of a fixed amount can be applied for for articles and books. The calculation is based on publications resulting from DFG-funded research. In the application year 2027, the grant is €1,400 per article. For open-access books that demonstrably result from a DFG-funded project, up to €5,000 per title can be applied for. The DFG may adjust the grant amount annually. Grants can generally only be applied for by research institutions. Individual researchers are only eligible to apply if they receive DFG funding but are not affiliated with an eligible institution or have additional needs, such as image licenses. The funding period for research institutions is one year."

title: DCAT-US Schema v3.0 | resources.data.gov
content:
"DCAT-US v3.0 is the federal data catalog metadata standard, updated to improve the Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability (FAIRness) of federal data. It is a U.S. application profile of the W3C Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT) version 3 — not a new or separate standard. This means most DCAT-US v3.0 metadata is valid W3C DCAT 3 metadata, making it easier to share federal data with international catalogs and platforms that understand the W3C standard.

DCAT-US v3.0 was developed collaboratively by the Federal Chief Data Officers Council, the Federal Committee on Statistical Methodology, and the Data.gov team at GSA, drawing on more than a decade of implementation experience with v1.1 and feedback from agencies, data providers, and data users across government. The schema is maintained in a public GitHub repository and governed through a CDO Tiger Team review process to ensure ongoing accuracy and responsiveness to agency needs."

title: OAPEN and Max Planck Society partner to build collection of funded open access books - MPDL
content:
"The OAPEN Foundation is delighted to announce a new partnership with the Max Planck Society (MPG) to build a dedicated collection of open access books funded by more than 80 Max Planck Institutes (MPIs) and research facilities.

The Institutes and research facilities range in expertise, from natural and life sciences to the humanities. The collection will provide MPG with comprehensive oversight of open access books funded by its institutes or centrally via the Max Planck Digital Library (MPDL). Max Planck-affiliated authors will also benefit from increased dissemination of their open access books.

The partnership marks an important step in extending OAPEN’s collection services beyond research funders to support research institutions, helping them to gain greater oversight of their open access book outputs and funded publishing activities.

It also reflects the shared commitment of OAPEN and MPG to strengthening the visibility, discoverability, and long-term accessibility of open access books within the wider open science ecosystem, in Germany and beyond."

title: Open Research Manager (Open Access and Publishing) - AD2605
content:
"We are looking for a proactive, enthusiastic and highly skilled individual with expert knowledge of open access and scholarly publishing to join our Open Research team in Libraries & Museums at University of St Andrews. The purpose of this role is to focus on advocacy and outreach for Open Access (OA), and to manage staff and services which support the University’s open research culture. You will take responsibility for our journal hosting platform (Open Journal Systems) and our research information system (Pure) workflows for research outputs.

This is an exciting time to join Libraries & Museums as we promote our open research culture which values sustainable and equitable open access. You will share our commitment to making our research outputs as widely available as possible and continue to embed our institutional OA Policy based on rights retention.

We are looking for a natural leader who will take initiative to further develop our OA services. You will have excellent communication skills and the ability to solve problems with an evidence-based approach."

title: Sustaining trusted open access infrastructure: Thank you to our publisher and data user supporters – DOAJ Blog
content:
"DOAJ is supported by a diverse community of organisations that recognise the importance of trusted, open infrastructure for scholarly communication.

Our work depends on sustained investment in our people, systems and infrastructure. We are therefore very grateful to the publishers and data users who choose to support DOAJ and contribute to the costs of maintaining and developing the service.

Publishers that support DOAJ help sustain an infrastructure that provides quality assurance, visibility, and discoverability for open access journals around the world. Our editorial team assesses nearly 9,000 new applications each year, alongside ongoing quality checks and investigations into suspected bad practice. This work helps maintain trust in the journals included in DOAJ and supports the wider community in identifying trusted open access publishing."

title: Diamond Open Access? | Ubiquity Press
content: From Google's English: Abstract: This article adopts the organizational-theoretical concept of path dependency in open access for analysis. According to this concept, open access publishing is no longer described as a single path, but rather two paths must be fundamentally distinguished, and their relationship to one another analyzed. While the commercial path of open access is now perceived as resistant to transformation, hopes are now pinned on a non-profit path (Diamond Open Access), which is organizationally distinct. The efforts to expand non-commercial publishing infrastructures are a reaction to the transformation agreements with the currently dominant publishing oligopoly. Among the numerous undesirable consequences of these agreements are the continued prevalence of hybrid publishing, the largely absent transformation from the subscription model to gold open access journals, the redistribution of acquisition and publication funds among funding institutions to the benefit of the oligopoly, and thus, overall, a deepening of dependence on publishers. title: FAIR Clinics: from principles to practice
content:
"Join us for our half-day event focused on bringing FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) practices to everyday medical research.

This year marks 10 years since the introduction of the FAIR principles. Over the past decade, much has been achieved - but for many researchers, FAIR can still feel abstract and difficult to translate into daily practice. Many recognize its importance but continue to face a simple question Where do I start?

This event is designed to answer exactly that!

We introduce FAIR Clinics - short, hands-on sessions where you will actively work on concrete outputs relevant to your research. The attention is not just on why FAIR matters, but on how to get started in practice."

title: Motivation and concerns regarding the use of preprints among Brazilian health researchers: a survey | medRxiv
content: Abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the motivations and concerns related to preprint use among Brazilian health researchers. A mixed-methods online survey of all 1,596 holders of CNPq Research Productivity Grants in seven health fields was conducted in 2025. The questionnaire was adapted from a survey of bioRxiv authors, translated into Portuguese, and pilot-tested. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively, and free-text responses were grouped by similarity. Overall, 178 researchers accessed the survey (11.2%), and 143 answered items on preprints and were included in the final analysis (9.0% effective response rate). The mean age was 55.9 years, and 88.0% were affiliated with public institutions. Regarding corresponding-author publications over the previous five years, 62.2% of respondents had deposited no preprints, while 37.8% had deposited at least one. Among preprints users, 79.2% agreed that deposition was freely decided by the authors. The main motivations were rapid sharing of findings (69.8%) and obtaining feedback (49.1%). content: "Participating in Publish-Review-Curate publishing requires that "Publish" infrastructures - repositories and preprint servers - provide robust version support, since this is required to ensure coherence in the PRC landscape. After a review of current practices, we are asking for feedback from PRC practitioners and repositories about the practices we have identified, what works best from your perspective, and whether we have missed anything important. Please provide your comments directly in this google document or by sending them to kathleen.shearer@coar-repositories.org by the end of September."
